title: When a marriage ends
hookLine: the Church accompanies divorced people; nullity is a separate question explained by the parish
tomorrow: is 'one day at a time' in the Bible, or just a slogan?

cards: A best friend's parents are splitting up. Her mom, who hasn't been to Mass in a while, says quietly that the Church probably doesn't want her now. She's been sitting in the parking lot on Sundays, then driving home.
Divorced means out; that's what she's heard. It's a common thing to hear. It isn't what the Church says.

teach.b: Jesus sets the bar for marriage high, in the Douay-Rheims: "What therefore God hath joined together, let no man put asunder." The Church holds to that, and still refuses to shut the door on people whose marriages end.

Pope Francis wrote, in The Joy of Love, that divorced people who haven't remarried should be encouraged to find strength in the Eucharist, and that those who are divorced and remarried are not excommunicated and belong in the community's life.
One to tell a friend: a declaration of nullity, what people call an annulment, is a separate question. It isn't a Catholic divorce.
It's a Church court's finding that something needed for a valid marriage was missing from the start, and Church law says the children of such a marriage are legitimate.
The parish explains it, case by case; nobody has to settle it at a kitchen table.
And this week's lines all hold here too. A marriage ending is pain carried together.
Help is holy. And fear, for a kid caught in the middle, deserves gentleness.

how: Parishes welcome divorced Catholics to Mass and parish life, and some run support groups for the separated and divorced; questions about a declaration of nullity go to a priest or the diocesan tribunal.

games.q: what does “when a marriage ends” mean?
o: a marriage's end, met by a Church that keeps you
a family moving away to a new parish
the moment a couple renews their wedding vows

games.q: this week's lines, and today's — tap the pairs.
p: a separate question, explained by the parish

s: Pope Francis wrote that divorced and remarried people are not excommunicated
The Joy of Love: they belong in the community's life. still in the family.
an annulment is a Catholic divorce that makes the children illegitimate
it's a finding that something was missing from the start, and Church law calls the children legitimate.
back from yesterday: the Church entrusts these children to God's mercy, with hope.

games.q: at the parish fish fry, someone whispers that the divorced woman serving at the counter 'shouldn't be up front.' what fits today?
o: she belongs here. divorced people are still part of the parish family.
he has a point; divorce means stepping back from parish life.
it depends on whether she's had an annulment yet.
games.why: the Church holds marriage permanent and still keeps divorced people in its family. nullity is a separate question, not a ticket back in.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose marriage ended: a parent, a friend, maybe you. Say their first name out loud, softly. Then hold them in mind for a while without trying to fix anything.
If you pray, you can pray for them, and for any children in the middle.

wordCard.voice: When a marriage ends. A real loss, met by a Church that keeps divorced people in its family and leaves nullity to the parish to explain. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: nothingness, invalidity. the root of a declaration of nullity, what people call an annulment.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: still in the family, whatever the paperwork says. That's the week.
